newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet hearing zeroes in on FAA staff shortages.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet hearing zeroes in on FAA staff shortages.

text.p: Investigators probing the crash of ValuJet Flight 592 on Thursday zeroed in on the inability of aviation regulators to keep up with inspections and paperwork during the low-cost carrier's explosive growth.

Two Federal Aviation Administration inspectors assigned to oversee ValuJet testified that the carrier's growth had raised alarms months before the crash, but staff shortages did not allow thorough inspection of the airline and its contractors.
"What I heard today disturbs me greatly," said hearing chairman John Goglia. "I saw a bunch of people struggling to do an impossible job."

The testimony came on the fourth day of a National Transportation Safety Board hearing into the crash of a ValuJet DC-9 that plunged into Florida's Everglades near Miami on Moy 11, killing all 110 passengers and crew on board.
Inspector Robert Bruce said he was certifying so many new aircraft and pilots he did not have time to immediately review changes in the airline's operating procedures.

He said ValuJet had 40 pilots a month finishing its training program at one point last year, taking up virtually all the time of one FAA inspector. But he said he never considered slowing the company's growth to get inspection procedures back on track.

"I am troubled by your workload," Goglia said. "Any supervisor who is required to take home volumes of work to get the job done means something is wrong. You are not fulfilling your job and doing your duty to the flying public if you cannot see the forest because you're buried in the trees."
Relatives of passengers and crew killed in the crash who attended the session applauded Goglia's remarks, their first spontaneous outburst of emotion in the four days of hearings.

On Wednesday, a group of relatives accused the FAA of failing to oversee airlines properly and demanded the government require all airlines to install smoke detectors and fire suppression equipment in airplane cargo holds.
Investigators believe oxygen canisters improperly packed by ValuJet maintenance contractor SabreTech and loaded aboard the plane may have started or fueled a fire in the hold.
Dave Harper, the FAA inspector responsible for overseeing maintenance at ValuJet, said he had concerns about ValuJet's explosive growth as much as a year before the accident.
"The growth of the carrier was pretty breathtaking," he said. "I had some concerns about the ability of the company to stay ahead of the business."

Yet with only a few inspectors to watch over 52 aircraft, 4,000 employees and 21 maintenance facilities contracted with ValuJet, Harper said he was unable to visit most of them and had inspected SabreTech in Miami just once, for 2-3 hours.
